Finish the open tween instantly, then play the close tween

cautions: os.Rename is not atomic on non-Unix platforms.
Checksums catch corruption, not deliberate tampering.
designGuide.cost: A struct and a migration function per format version, one fixture per release, and a few extra system calls on every save.
strengths: Old saves keep loading as the format evolves.
A crash during saving never destroys progress.

readings.hint: Picture the file if power fails halfway through the write.
readings.introduction: A save file outlives the build that wrote it, sits in a folder the player can edit and gets shared on forums. A loader that unmarshals it straight into game state will eventually meet a save from an older version, a save from a newer version, a file truncated by a crash and a hand-edited file with 999 health. Each of those needs a deliberate answer, and none of them should be a panic.
readings.nuance: On POSIX file systems rename swaps the directory entry in one step, so readers see the complete old save or the complete synced new one; writing in place truncates first and can leave a torn file.
readings.objective: Design a versioned JSON save format, migrate v1 saves to v2, reject unknown fields and out-of-range values, and replace a save file without ever leaving it half-written.
readings.question: Why does the save code write to a temporary file in the same directory and then rename it over the old save?
readings.reviewAnswer: A crash leaves the old or new file, never half of each
readings.reviewPrompt: Why temp file + rename for saves?

sections.body: Old files: a field was renamed or restructured, the new struct silently decodes it as zero, and a v1 player loads with 0 health. Newer files: a player downgrades or copies a save from a newer build, the old build drops fields it does not know and then overwrites the file with less data than it read. Torn files: the game crashes or the device loses power during a write, and the only save is part old and part new. Crafted files: someone sets an inventory count to a billion or adds an item that does not exist, and the game indexes past a slice or grants a debug item. The answers are a version field read first, pure migration functions, strict decoding followed by explicit validation, and an atomic replace when writing.
sections.title: Four ways a naive loader fails

sections.body: The program loads a v1 save (flat hp, a position array and a list of item names) and migrates it to v2 (structured health, a position object and item stacks). It loads a valid v2 save, then feeds the loader six bad files: an unknown field, impossible health, a position outside the map, an unknown item, a newer version and a file with a second JSON value appended. Finally it writes the last good save atomically into a fresh directory under os.TempDir, reloads it and confirms that no temporary file was left behind.
sections.title: Decode the version, migrate, then validate
sections.walkthrough: Load caps the input at 64 KiB with io.LimitReader before parsing anything. json.Unmarshal into a struct holding only the version reads the version and, because Unmarshal requires exactly one JSON value, also rejects the file with trailing data; a json.Decoder alone would stop after the first value and never notice it. The switch then decodes with a Decoder whose DisallowUnknownFields turns godMode into an error instead of silently ignoring it. migrateV1 is a pure function that groups items into stacks in first-seen order rather than through a map, so its output is stable. Validate checks every invariant the game relies on; the negated range test for position also rejects NaN produced by a buggy migration. WriteAtomic writes a temporary file in the destination directory, syncs it, closes it and renames it over the target, and the deferred cleanup removes the temporary file if any step fails.

sections.body: Each release that changes the format gets a new struct and one function from the previous version to the next. Loading a v1 file in a v4 build runs v1 to v2, v2 to v3 and v3 to v4, so each migration is written and tested once against its own fixtures and never needs to know about later versions. Migrations choose defaults explicitly: v1 had no maximum health, so the function writes 100 rather than letting a zero value slip through. Refuse versions newer than the build supports, because a downgraded game that loads a v3 file into v2 structs and saves it back destroys progress. Do not rewrite the original file on load; write the migrated save on the next normal save through the atomic path, and keep the previous file as a backup slot until the new one has loaded successfully once. Note that encoding/json matches field names case-insensitively and lets a repeated key overwrite the earlier one; the strict JSON lesson shows the encoding/json/v2 options that reject both when a format needs it.
sections.title: Migrate forward in small, pure steps

sections.body: Writing a save in place truncates the file first, so a crash mid-write leaves neither version. Writing a temporary file in the same directory and renaming it over the old one gives readers either the complete old file or the complete new one, because on POSIX file systems rename replaces the directory entry in one step. The temporary file must live in the same directory, since a rename across file systems fails. Call Sync before Close so the bytes are durable before the name points at them, and on Unix also sync the directory if the rename itself must survive a power cut. The os.Rename documentation states that on non-Unix platforms it is not atomic even within one directory, so a Windows build should keep a backup slot and verify the new file on load. Console and mobile platforms usually provide save APIs with their own guarantees; prefer them there.
sections.title: Atomic replace: what rename does and does not promise
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs at the end of a function like WriteAtomic, runs in your own native environment and applies to Unix systems. Opening the parent directory and calling Sync asks the file system to persist the directory entry that rename changed; without it, a power loss right after the rename can bring back the old name on some file systems. It does not replace the Sync on the file itself, which persists the contents.

sections.body: Decoding proves only that the bytes matched the struct shape. Validation proves the game can use the result: ranges for every number, existence for every reference such as item IDs or level names, limits on every collection, and cross-field rules such as current health at most maximum health. Decide per field whether to reject the save or repair it with a logged clamp; rejecting is safer for anything that indexes memory, repairing is kinder for cosmetic settings. A checksum detects accidental corruption but is not tamper protection, because any key shipped in the client can be extracted; competitive or economy data belongs on a server. Keep a fixture directory with one real save from every released version and load all of them in CI, then fuzz the loader with those fixtures as the seed corpus.
sections.title: Validate after decoding, and test the loader like a parser
sections.walkthrough: This test fragment lives in a _test.go file in your own module and runs with go test -fuzz=FuzzLoad on your machine; fixtureSaves is your helper that reads the fixture directory. The property is simple and strong: for any bytes, Load either returns an error or returns a save that passes Validate, and it never panics, hangs or allocates without bound. Crashing inputs found by the fuzzer are written under testdata/fuzz and become permanent regression cases.

readings.takeaway: Read the version first, migrate with pure per-version functions, decode strictly and validate every invariant, refuse newer formats, and replace saves by renaming a synced temporary file from the same directory.
readings.title: Save files are untrusted input: version them, migrate forward, validate and write atomically
wrongAnswers: It stops players from editing the save between sessions
os.WriteFile cannot replace a file that already exists

cautions: A blocking broadcast lets one slow client stall the tick.
Strict rules without tolerance punish lossy connections.
designGuide.cost: Server CPU for every player's simulation, a round trip of latency the client must hide, and a validation rule for every action.
strengths: A modified client cannot teleport or exceed the speed cap.
One owner goroutine removes locks from game logic.

readings.hint: Which side decides where a modified client ends up?
readings.introduction: In a multiplayer game every client is a program you do not control. If clients report their own positions, a modified client can teleport, fly or walk through walls, and the server has no grounds to refuse. An authoritative server inverts that: clients send what the player wants to do, the server decides what happens, and everyone receives the server's version of the world. Goroutines and channels fit this shape well, provided exactly one goroutine owns the state.
readings.nuance: With directions the server applies its own speed cap, collision and bounds, so a hacked client can at most choose where to walk; a reported position would let the client decide the outcome.
readings.objective: Build a server tick loop in which one goroutine owns all game state, clients send inputs over channels, movement is validated against speed and rate limits, and snapshots are copies in a deterministic order.
readings.question: Why does the authoritative server accept movement directions from clients instead of positions?
readings.reviewAnswer: Inputs with sequence numbers; the server computes moves
readings.reviewPrompt: What should a game client send?

sections.body: An input message carries a sequence number and a desired direction. It has no position, health or score field, so there is nothing to forge. The server tick applies inputs with its own speed, its own collision rules from the previous unit and its own map, then publishes a snapshot. Ownership is the other half of the design: the world lives in one goroutine. Network readers and timers talk to it through channels, and nothing outside that goroutine holds a pointer into the world. That removes locks from game logic, makes each tick a sequential function you can review and test, and gives every rule a single place to be enforced. The sender's identity comes from the connection, never from a field in the payload.
sections.title: Clients send intent; the server computes outcomes

sections.body: The program starts a server goroutine that owns three players, creates one Session per simulated client and runs four ticks. In each tick every client goroutine sends its inputs concurrently; the main goroutine waits for all sends, asks the server for a tick and prints the snapshot. Player 1 walks right, player 2 uses keyboard diagonals and then turns, and player 3 cheats with an oversized direction, three moves in one tick, a replayed sequence number, a NaN direction and a forged player ID.
sections.title: A tick loop with validation and deterministic order
sections.walkthrough: Inputs travel over an unbuffered channel, so each Send completes only when the server goroutine has received the value, and wg.Wait therefore proves that every input is in pending before the tick request is sent. Arrival order still depends on the scheduler, so step sorts by player and sequence before applying anything, and the output is identical on every run. apply drops a sequence at or below the last one seen, allows one move per player per tick, rejects non-finite directions and normalizes any direction longer than 1, logging only lengths that no real controller produces. Dropped extras still advance the ack so the client stops resending them. Positions are clamped to the arena, which is why player 3 stops at 100.0. Session overwrites Player, so player 3's attempt to send as player 1 just moves player 3. Snapshots copy values into PlayerState, so no client can alias server memory.

sections.body: Every rule needs a tolerance chosen with real networks in mind. Packets get duplicated and reordered, so an old sequence number is dropped quietly rather than treated as an attack. A burst of inputs after a lag spike is normal: a production server usually queues a few inputs per player and applies them over the next ticks, dropping only beyond that budget, whereas this program drops extras immediately to stay short. Normalizing direction vectors means a gamepad, a keyboard and a hacked client all move at the same maximum speed without the server guessing intent. Record violations with player, tick and sequence, and act on rates over time rather than on one event, because a single odd input is far more often a bug or a bad connection than a cheat. Never use a client-reported position even as a hint; if client and server disagree, the server is right and the client is corrected, which is the subject of the next lesson.
sections.title: Validation rules that do not punish honest players

sections.body: The program drives ticks by hand to stay deterministic. A real server replaces the tick request with a time.Ticker and broadcasts each snapshot to per-client channels. The broadcast must never wait for a slow client: a full channel means that client misses this snapshot and gets the next one, which is harmless when each snapshot carries complete state rather than a delta.
sections.title: The production loop: a ticker, one select and non-blocking fan-out
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own native environment; its ticks come from the wall clock, so its output is not reproducible the way the program's is. Joins arrive as messages in the same select, so the clients slice is touched only by the owner goroutine, and leaves would work the same way. Each client has a small buffered snapshots channel drained by its own writer goroutine that encodes and sends; all writers read the same snapshot, so treat it as immutable once published. A time.Ticker drops ticks when the receiver falls behind instead of queueing them, so measure each tick's duration and alert when it approaches the interval.

sections.body: The tick loop does not care whether inputs come from an in-process Session, UDP datagrams or WebSocket messages. Fast-paced games usually prefer UDP because a lost packet should not hold newer inputs back the way in-order TCP delivery does. The reader goroutine does the untrusted-input work: size limits, decoding, mapping the sender to an authenticated session, and dropping instead of blocking when the server is busy.
sections.title: A real transport feeds the same channel
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment with a conn from net.ListenPacket("udp", ":7777"); Sessions, decodeInput and the handshake are yours to define. A source address alone is not authentication, because UDP source addresses can be spoofed, so Verify checks a per-session token or message authentication code agreed during an authenticated connect. Ignoring unknown senders without replying keeps the server from becoming a traffic amplifier. The buffer is reused across reads, which is safe because decodeInput copies values into an Input before the next ReadFrom. A WebSocket transport, which needs a third-party package because the standard library has none, would feed the same channel.

sections.body: Most server logic lives in step, a function of world state and a batch of inputs. Test it directly with tables of inputs and expected snapshots, including the cheats from the program, duplicated and reordered sequences, players joining and leaving between ticks, and inputs for unknown players. Run the goroutine wrapper under the race detector to prove nothing else touches the world, and fuzz decodeInput with arbitrary bytes. Then add a few integration tests over a loopback socket with injected latency and loss; they are slower and noisier, but they catch framing and shutdown bugs. This model runs in one process. A production server adds authentication, matchmaking, persistence, interest management so each client receives only nearby entities, and metrics for tick duration and per-client drops.
sections.title: Test the tick, not the network

readings.takeaway: Let one goroutine own the world, accept only intent with sequence numbers, take identity from the connection, validate direction, rate and order every tick, sort inputs before applying them, and publish copied snapshots without blocking on slow clients.

Directions let clients keep moving while the server is busy

cautions: Prediction needs identical movement code on both sides.
Remote players are shown in the past; hits need lag compensation.
designGuide.cost: A pending-input buffer, a snapshot buffer and replay work proportional to the round-trip time on every snapshot.
strengths: Local movement responds on the same tick as the input.
Corrections are limited to real server disagreement.

readings.hint: The server has not applied some of the inputs yet; which ones still matter?
readings.introduction: The authoritative server from the previous lesson is fair but feels slow. With 50 ms of latency each way, a player presses right and nothing moves for a tenth of a second. Client-side prediction runs the same movement rule locally so the press responds at once, reconciliation fixes the prediction when the server disagrees, and interpolation shows other players smoothly, slightly in the past. They solve three different problems with three different pieces of state.
readings.nuance: Inputs 4 to 8 are still in flight and the server will apply them; replaying them on top of the authoritative state predicts where the server will be and corrects only real disagreements, such as the closed door.
readings.objective: Hide round-trip latency by predicting local movement, reconcile with acknowledged server snapshots by replaying pending inputs, and draw remote players by interpolating a snapshot buffer.
readings.question: A snapshot arrives with the server position and ack = 3 while the client has already sent inputs up to 8. What should the client do?
readings.reviewAnswer: Reset to server state, replay inputs after the ack

sections.body: Prediction needs the local player's predicted state and a buffer of inputs that were sent but not yet acknowledged. Reconciliation needs each snapshot to carry the server's state for this player plus the last input sequence the server applied, the ack. Interpolation needs a short buffer of snapshots of the remote entities, each tagged with its server tick. The local player is drawn at the predicted present; everyone else is drawn at a deliberate point in the past, where two real snapshots surround the render time. Mixing those up causes familiar bugs: predicting remote players makes them jitter and snap whenever they change direction, and interpolating your own character makes the controls feel delayed.
sections.title: Three techniques, three pieces of client state

sections.body: The program simulates both ends in one loop, with a one-way latency of 3 ticks and a snapshot every 2 ticks. The client presses right for ten ticks. At server tick 5 a door at x = 6 closes, which the client cannot predict. A second player runs right for five ticks and then turns back. Each snapshot arrival prints the reconciliation, and the remote lines show what the client draws for the other player next to what was true at that moment and what is true now.
sections.title: A deterministic network with fixed latency
sections.walkthrough: Predict appends the input to pending and moves immediately with the shared Move function. Reconcile resets to the snapshot's position and door state, keeps only inputs after the ack and replays them. Until the door closes the replay lands exactly on the prediction, so the correction is 0.0. At t=9 the snapshot from server tick 6 reports x=3.0, ack 3 and a closed door; replaying inputs 4 to 8 stops at the door, so the predicted 8.0 is corrected by 2.0 and later predictions stay at 6.0. The remote player is drawn at server time t - latency - interpDelay. At t=10 that is time 5, between the snapshots for ticks 4 and 6, which are both 18.0, so the true peak of 20.0 never appears: interpolation smooths over events that fall between snapshots. After the last ack, pending is empty and client and server agree.

sections.body: Snapping to the server position without a replay would discard every input still in flight and pull the character back by a full round trip on every snapshot. Replaying pending inputs on top of the authoritative state keeps corrections small: only the part the server actually disagreed with changes. That works only if client and server run the same movement code, which is easy in Go when both binaries import one simulation package. Bound the pending buffer to a few hundred milliseconds of inputs and treat overflow as a broken connection. Ignore any snapshot older than one already applied; this program never needs that check because its link never reorders. Keep the simulation state snapped to the corrected value, but let the rendered position chase it over a few frames, so a 2-unit correction looks like a slight drift rather than a teleport, and snap the rendered position too when the error is large, such as after a respawn.
sections.title: Reconcile by replaying, then smooth what the player sees

sections.body: The client never sees other players' inputs, so it cannot predict them well. Instead it draws them at a render time behind the newest snapshot and interpolates between the two snapshots that bracket it. The delay must cover the snapshot interval plus network jitter; many games use two intervals so that one lost packet does not empty the buffer, while this program uses one to keep the output short. When the buffer runs dry, hold the last position or extrapolate for a short, capped time, then hold. The delay has a visible cost: you see opponents where they were, so a shot aimed at them would miss on the server unless the server performs lag compensation, rewinding other players to the moment the shooter saw before testing the hit. That decision is a fairness trade-off between shooter and target, and it belongs on the server, never in the client.
sections.title: Remote players live in the past on purpose

sections.body: Prediction tolerates small divergence because reconciliation corrects it. Lockstep networking, where peers exchange only inputs, does not: it needs bit-identical simulation on every machine, which in Go means iterating slices instead of maps, avoiding goroutine-dependent order and remembering that floating-point fusion can differ between arm64 and amd64 builds. Test netcode the way this program runs: a simulated link with configurable latency, jitter, loss and reordering driven by a seeded generator, with no sockets and no sleeps. Assert convergence, meaning that after inputs stop and messages drain, client and server agree and pending is empty; assert zero corrections when no server-only event happens; and assert bounded corrections when one does. Then add adversarial schedules: a snapshot lost right before the door event, two snapshots arriving in one tick and a snapshot older than one already applied.
sections.title: How much determinism you need, and how to test it

readings.takeaway: Predict the local player with shared movement code, keep unacknowledged inputs, reconcile by resetting to the server state and replaying inputs after the ack, and draw remote players interpolated between buffered snapshots at a fixed delay.

cautions: Non-zero allocation counts change between Go releases.
sync.Pool may drop pooled objects at any GC cycle.
designGuide.cost: Scratch fields on the world, capacity planning at level load, and code that is slightly less obvious than allocating fresh values.
strengths: A zero-allocation assertion catches regressions in CI.
Loop-owned buffers are deterministic and cache-friendly.

readings.hint: Think about which number a test can assert reliably across Go releases.
readings.introduction: At 60 frames per second each frame has about 16.6 ms for input, simulation, drawing and whatever the runtime needs. Go's garbage collector runs concurrently, but its work is paid for by your program: the more a game allocates per frame, the more often a cycle starts and the more CPU the collector takes from the loop. The useful goal is not zero allocations ever; it is an update that allocates nothing in steady state, verified by a number a test can check.
readings.nuance: Allocation rate drives how often GC cycles start and how much assist work the loop pays; an update that allocates nothing in steady state removes that pressure, and asserting exactly zero stays valid when releases change non-zero counts.
readings.objective: Turn refresh rates into frame budgets, count allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun, remove per-frame slices, maps, closures and strings, and profile a game loop with pprof and execution traces.
readings.question: What allocation target should a game's per-frame update have, and how do you keep it there?
readings.reviewAnswer: Zero in steady state, enforced by an AllocsPerRun test

sections.body: Divide one second by the refresh rate: about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz and 6.9 ms at 144 Hz. Ebitengine calls Update at the tick rate and Draw once per displayed frame, and both share that budget with the graphics driver and the operating system. A frame that misses its deadline is a visible hitch, and players notice a single 30 ms spike more than a steady 10 ms average. Allocation feeds that risk. The collector paces cycles by heap growth, so a loop that allocates a few megabytes per second starts cycles regularly; during a cycle, background workers take a share of the CPU and goroutines that keep allocating are charged assist work, which lands directly in your update. Reducing the allocation rate is therefore the first lever, and GOGC or GOMEMLIMIT tuning, covered by the GC budget lesson, comes after it.
sections.title: Where the 16.6 ms goes

sections.body: testing.AllocsPerRun runs a function once to warm up, counts heap allocations over the requested number of runs and returns the integer average, with GOMAXPROCS set to 1 during the measurement. It works outside tests too, so the program uses it on paired implementations: a visibility query written the obvious way and one that reuses storage, deferred hit effects as closures and as values, and HUD text rebuilt every update versus cached. The two versions in each pair produce the same result; only their allocation behavior differs.
sections.title: Count allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun
sections.walkthrough: time.Second / time.Duration(hz) prints exact budgets. VisibleFresh allocates 22 times per call: append growing a nil slice to 173 elements, the map growing as IDs are inserted, and sort.Slice, which receives the slice as an interface and builds a reflection-based swapper. VisibleReuse truncates a slice sized at level load, replaces the map with a stamp slice compared against a frame counter and sorts with slices.SortFunc; its comparison closure captures w but does not escape, so it lives on the stack and the count is 0. QueueClosures stores 32 capturing closures in a slice for later, so each one escapes to the heap: exactly 32. QueueValues queues the same hits as structs: 0. fmt.Sprintf allocates twice, once to box the int into its ...any parameter and once for the new string, while the HUD cache rebuilds only when the score changes. Results go into package-level variables so the compiler cannot discard the work. The counts are stable for one toolchain but can change between Go releases as escape analysis improves.

sections.body: Size scratch slices when a level loads and reuse them with s = s[:0], so append writes into existing capacity. Replace per-frame sets with data the world already owns: a stamp slice, a bit set, or a long-lived map emptied with clear(m), which keeps its storage. Queue effects as plain structs processed in one loop instead of closures that capture entities; values are also easier to log, replay and send over the network. Closures are not the problem by themselves, escaping closures are: a closure passed to a function that only calls it, like the SortFunc comparator, stays on the stack. Watch for hidden boxing, because passing an int or a struct as any to fmt, a logger or an interface-typed event bus can allocate, and so can converting []byte to string for text. Build HUD strings when the value changes, not every frame. To see why a line allocates, go build -gcflags=-m prints the compiler's escape decisions.
sections.title: Patterns that keep the steady state allocation-free

sections.body: sync.Pool helps when many goroutines need short-lived buffers, such as a server encoding snapshots for hundreds of clients in parallel. It is a poor fit for game entities. The pool may drop any object during garbage collection, keeping one victim generation so an idle object survives about one extra cycle at most; Get may return a fresh object; and every Get and Put adds ownership rules, which the pool ownership lesson covers. A single-threaded update loop has a simpler, deterministic option: a free list. Keep particles or projectiles in a slice, mark dead ones and push their indexes onto a free list that the next spawn pops. Nothing is allocated once capacity is reached, nothing disappears behind your back, and iterating a dense slice is friendly to the CPU cache.
sections.title: sync.Pool or a free list owned by the loop
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs to an update loop in your own game and runs in your native environment; Particle is your struct with an Alive flag that the update skips. Spawn reuses a dead slot before growing items, so once items and free reach their working capacity, spawning and killing allocate nothing. Kill must run once per particle, and other systems that hold an index can see a reused slot; a generation counter per slot, checked on every lookup, catches those stale indexes. Choose sync.Pool when objects cross goroutines and reuse is only an optimization, and a free list when the loop owns them.

sections.body: A number printed once is a curiosity; a test that fails when the hot path starts allocating is a guard. Assert exactly zero rather than a non-zero count, because zero stays valid when a Go release changes escape analysis. Pair it with a benchmark that reports time and allocations per update for a scripted scene with a fixed seed, so two runs are comparable.
sections.title: Turn the measurement into a test and a benchmark
sections.walkthrough: This fragment goes into a _test.go file beside your World type and runs with go test in your own module. The explicit warm-up call lets scratch slices reach their working capacity before measuring; AllocsPerRun also warms up once on its own. Passing the method value w.Update is fine here because it is created once, outside the measured runs. b.Loop, available since Go 1.24, runs the body the right number of times and keeps the setup above it out of the timing. Run the zero-allocation test without -race and without coverage, since instrumentation can change the counts.

sections.body: When the budget is blown, benchmarks and profiles answer where the time goes and which lines allocate, and traces show whether a slow frame overlapped a GC cycle. Use the same deterministic scene for every comparison.
sections.code:
# Time and allocations per update, five samples for comparison
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -benchmem -count 5 ./game

# CPU and heap profiles from the same benchmark
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -cpuprofile cpu.out -memprofile mem.out ./game
go tool pprof -top cpu.out
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_objects -list 'World.Update' mem.out

# GC cycles while the real game runs, one line per cycle on stderr
GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./mygame 2> gc.log

# Execution trace: GC, goroutines and processor use on one timeline
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -trace trace.out ./game
go tool trace trace.out
sections.title: Profile the loop you actually ship
sections.walkthrough: Run these commands in your own module; ./game and ./mygame stand for your package and binary. -run '^$' skips ordinary tests so only benchmarks run. The heap profile written by -memprofile records allocation sites, and -sample_index=alloc_objects ranks them by count, which matches what AllocsPerRun measures; -list prints source lines with their numbers. gctrace prints one line per GC cycle while the game runs, and the execution trace puts GC, goroutines and processors on one timeline. For spikes that appear only in long sessions, runtime/trace's FlightRecorder keeps the last few seconds in memory, so a debug build can write it to a file when a frame exceeds its budget.

readings.takeaway: Budget each frame from the refresh rate, measure allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun, reach zero in steady state by reusing storage the loop owns, and confirm with benchmarks, pprof and traces before tuning the GC.
readings.title: A 16.6 ms frame budget: measure allocations per update and make the steady state allocate nothing
wrongAnswers: As few as possible, with runtime.GC called every frame
Any amount, since Go's concurrent GC never slows the loop

lessons.explanation: A game loop runs on two clocks. The display hands you frames of uneven length; the simulation should advance in identical steps. Decoupling the two with an accumulator makes physics independent of the frame rate, makes every run reproducible, and turns a long stall into bounded slow motion instead of a frozen game.
lessons.objective: Advance a simulation in fixed steps from variable frame times, draw it with an interpolation factor and cap catch-up work after a stall.
lessons.title: Fix the timestep: an accumulator turns uneven frames into identical simulation steps

lessons.explanation: Ebitengine runs the loop from the previous lesson for you. You implement three methods, Update, Draw and Layout, and the engine decides when to call each one. Getting that split right is the most important structural decision in an Ebitengine project: a single state change inside Draw makes the game run at a different speed on every monitor.
lessons.objective: Structure an Ebitengine game so every state change happens in Update, Draw is a read-only view, and the rules run headless in tests.
lessons.title: Ebitengine's Game interface: Update advances ticks, Draw only reads, Layout fixes the screen

lessons.explanation: Almost every line of 2D movement code adds, scales or measures a pair of numbers. A tiny vector type with value methods makes that code read like the math, rules out aliasing bugs and costs nothing measurable. Combined with fixed ticks, it lets you tune movement in units a designer can reason about: pixels per tick, and a drag factor applied once per tick.
lessons.objective: Write a small value-semantics vector type and move a body with normalized input, per-tick acceleration and drag that behave the same on every display.
lessons.title: A 2D vector value type: normalized input, acceleration and drag in per-tick units

lessons.explanation: Players do not press buttons on the exact tick the game expects. They press jump a few ticks before landing or a few ticks after running off a ledge, and a strict implementation swallows those presses and feels broken. Responsive platformer controls are built from three small pieces: an action layer over physical keys, edge detection on actions, and short grace windows measured in ticks.
lessons.objective: Map physical keys to actions, detect presses on the action level, and implement jump buffering and coyote time as tick counters that can be tested deterministically.
lessons.title: Input as actions: edge detection, jump buffering and coyote time in a tick-exact simulation

lessons.explanation: Games are full of modes: menus, gameplay, pause overlays, and enemies that patrol, chase and attack. Encoding them as booleans such as paused, gameOver, chasing and attacking creates combinations that should be impossible and guards that must be repeated everywhere. Two explicit state machines replace them: a stack of scenes for the flow of the game, and one mode value with one transition function for each enemy.
lessons.objective: Run title, playing, paused and game-over scenes through a scene interface and a transition stack, and drive an enemy with a single-mode behavior machine.
lessons.title: Scenes and enemy behavior as explicit state machines instead of boolean flags

lessons.explanation: The first instinct for game objects is a hierarchy: a base object, a character built on it, an enemy built on that. In Go such hierarchies fight the language, which has no inheritance, and the hardware, which prefers contiguous data. An entity-component design keeps an entity as a bare ID, stores each component type in its own dense slice, and writes behavior as systems that loop over those slices.
lessons.objective: Build a minimal entity-component store with generics, run systems over dense slices, remove with swap-delete, and judge when plain structs are the better design.
lessons.title: Entities as IDs, components in dense generic stores, systems as plain loops

lessons.explanation: Collision handling has two jobs: detect that two shapes overlap, and decide how to move them apart. Axis-aligned boxes and circles cover most 2D games, and both have exact tests that cost a few comparisons. The failure that bites later is speed: an object that moves farther in one tick than an obstacle is thick can pass through it without ever overlapping it.
lessons.objective: Test boxes and circles for overlap, compute the minimum push that separates them, and stop fast objects from tunneling with sub-steps or a swept test.
lessons.title: AABB and circle collisions: detect overlap, push out along the shallow axis, sweep fast movers

lessons.explanation: Checking every object against every other costs n(n-1)/2 tests: 124,750 for 500 objects, every tick, and almost all of those pairs are far apart. A broad phase discards distant pairs cheaply so the exact tests from the collision lesson run only on near candidates. A uniform grid stored in a hash map is the simplest broad phase that works well for most 2D games.
lessons.objective: Build a uniform-grid spatial hash, insert objects by bounding box, query neighbors with deduplication, and count pair checks against the naive all-pairs loop.
lessons.title: A spatial hash for the broad phase: bucket by cell, query neighbors, check each pair once

lessons.explanation: The previous unit gave every entity a world position and a fixed-timestep update. A tile map lays a grid over that world, and a camera decides which part of it reaches the screen. Both are small pieces of arithmetic, and most tile-map bugs are one of three mistakes in it: the wrong coordinate space, the wrong rounding or the wrong edge.
lessons.objective: Convert between tile, world and screen coordinates, keep a following camera inside the map and compute the exact range of tiles to draw.
lessons.title: A camera is a coordinate transform: follow the target, clamp to the map, draw only visible tiles

lessons.explanation: Chasing the player in a straight line works until the first wall. Breadth-first search finds a way around but ignores terrain cost; Dijkstra respects cost but explores every cell closer than the goal, in all directions. A* keeps Dijkstra's guarantee while steering the search with an estimate of the remaining distance. Its quality depends on three choices that are easy to get subtly wrong: the cost model, the heuristic and the tie-break.
lessons.objective: Implement grid A* with container/heap, choose a heuristic that matches the movement rules, make equal-cost choices deterministic and decide when a flow field beats per-unit searches.
lessons.title: A* on a grid: a heap, a heuristic that matches the moves, and tie-breaking you can replay

lessons.explanation: Procedural generation is only useful when the same seed builds the same world: a player shares a seed, a tester attaches one to a bug report, a replay regenerates the level instead of storing it. That property is not automatic. It depends on who owns each random generator, how many values each system draws and in what order, and whether any code path reaches for a generator nobody seeded.
lessons.objective: Generate a seeded cave with a math/rand/v2 PCG source, keep each system on its own derived stream and explain why global or shared randomness breaks replays.
lessons.title: Reproducible worlds: one seed, one random stream per system, and no global rand

lessons.explanation: A panel slides in, a coin bounces, a character cycles through four walking frames. The tempting implementation reads time.Now in Draw and computes progress from it. That ties animation to the wall clock: it keeps running while the game is paused, it behaves differently at 60 Hz and 144 Hz, and a replay cannot reproduce it. The fixed-timestep loop from the previous unit already provides a better clock: the tick.
lessons.objective: Drive easing curves, chained and retargeted tweens and sprite animation clips from tick counts so motion is deterministic, pausable and free of jumps.
lessons.title: Tweens and sprite frames advance with the simulation tick, not the wall clock

lessons.explanation: A save file outlives the build that wrote it, sits in a folder the player can edit and gets shared on forums. A loader that unmarshals it straight into game state will eventually meet a save from an older version, a save from a newer version, a file truncated by a crash and a hand-edited file with 999 health. Each of those needs a deliberate answer, and none of them should be a panic.
lessons.objective: Design a versioned JSON save format, migrate v1 saves to v2, reject unknown fields and out-of-range values, and replace a save file without ever leaving it half-written.
lessons.title: Save files are untrusted input: version them, migrate forward, validate and write atomically

lessons.explanation: In a multiplayer game every client is a program you do not control. If clients report their own positions, a modified client can teleport, fly or walk through walls, and the server has no grounds to refuse. An authoritative server inverts that: clients send what the player wants to do, the server decides what happens, and everyone receives the server's version of the world. Goroutines and channels fit this shape well, provided exactly one goroutine owns the state.
lessons.objective: Build a server tick loop in which one goroutine owns all game state, clients send inputs over channels, movement is validated against speed and rate limits, and snapshots are copies in a deterministic order.
lessons.title: An authoritative server owns the world in one goroutine and accepts only validated intent

lessons.title: Client prediction replays unacknowledged inputs; remote players are interpolated from the past
